I haven't had time to review this PR in detail, but I'll just pop in to say that HTML is a mess with regards to these boolean and pseudo-boolean attributes. If this attribute can be a normal boolean attribute, that'd be simplest, but if it needs to be something pseudo-boolean, your choices are:

- `autocapitalize`: `on`, `off`, 4 other values
- `autocomplete`: `on`, `off`, tons of other values (but on `form` only those 2)
- `contenteditable`: `true`, `false`, 1 other value
- `draggable`: `true`, `false`
- `spellcheck`: `true`, `false`
- `translate`: `yes`, `no`

You can be a normal boolean attribute if you're truly 2 state (no other states, including a hidden third state like `draggable`, `spellcheck`, and `translate` have), and if your default is false/off/no. It looks like that is not the case here due to some inheritance behavior.

I think I agree with @mfreed7 that the `draggable` and `spellcheck` pattern of `true`/`false`, with custom boolean-ish reflection, is the best fit.

body:
The main reason for doing this way was to account for inheritance. Being able to control writing suggestions for the whole document (by setting the attribute on the document element) as well as on a single element are both important to developers. In addition, I'm not sure if all UAs will want to use an on-by-default state for writing suggestions. For `spellcheck` at least, Firefox's default is `false` for non-editable elements, but `true` for editable elements like `textarea`. That's why I worded the spec to allow the UA to establish a per-element default for `writingsuggestions` as well.

Another option was to do what `contenteditable` does: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-contenteditable, which is to return `inherit` as the default. The problem with that approach is that (1) `document.documentElement.contentEditable` returns `inherit` as well, which doesn't make much sense, and (2) an `inherit` value isn't informative to developers on whether the feature is enabled or not - it seems much more useful to get a value that represents the actual state post inheritance.

Even in that respect we're following the precedent for `spellcheck` here, which returns `true` even for element types that the spec says it can never apply to. The conditions under `User agents must only consider the following pieces of text as checkable...` do not affect the value of the `spellcheck` attribute.

A practical reason not to do this is that different UAs may make different decisions about where to support writing suggestions, e.g. some may support them in `input type="text"` elements and some may not. Either behavior is allowed per spec, and we don't want to expose these specific choices for the aforementioned privacy/fingerprinting reasons. So if developers get in the habit of checking `writingSuggestions` on different element types to see where it is supported, they could get the wrong idea about where a particular UA will end up providing writing suggestions.
